case_studies.title: HydroJEV: A one-second, training-free screen for cyber-attack and fault attribution in water distribution networks
case_studies.abstract: When a SCADA alarm is raised in a water distribution network, operators must decide quickly whether it reflects a cyberattack, a physical fault, a normal transient or a faulty sensor. Supervised classifiers need labelled incidents that utilities rarely have, and frontier large language models (LLMs) take tens of seconds per decision. We tested whether Jev, a training-free model that returns class probabilities in about one second, can serve as the first tier of this triage. case_studies.summary: When a SCADA alarm pops up in a water network, operators need to know fast if it’s a cyberattack, a physical fault, a normal glitch or a bad sensor. The authors built Jev, a training‑free model that gives a cause probability in about one second, eliminating the need for labelled data or slow LLMs. Jev achieved competitive accuracy on a four‑class benchmark for the C‑Town water network.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage SCADA or OT monitoring, you can add Jev as a first‑pass triage: 1) feed the alarm data into Jev to get instant cause probabilities; 2) use the top suggestion to trigger the appropriate incident response; 3) log the outcome for future training or audit. This reduces manual triage time and improves response accuracy.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a training-free, one-second model for attributing cyber-attacks in water distribution SCADA systems. While technically interesting, the scope is highly specialized to industrial control systems in water utilities, which is peripheral to the typical Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Okta, AWS, Azure, and endpoint management environments of the target audience. The novelty is limited to a niche domain, offering little cross-application to common IT infrastructures. There is no direct actionable content for immediate automation or risk flagging within the next 90 days for general IT engineers. Consequently, the total score falls below 40, and low_signal is set to true.

case_studies.title: PACE: Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement for Tool-Using LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents turn generated text into real side effects, so poisoned tool metadata, retrieved pages, memory, and reusable skills can steer the next call. Vetting an artifact before admission does not settle this. A safe variant and a leaking variant can produce the same admission evidence, and a sound gate then cannot relax that site for either. We make that condition precise, which leaves the last boundary a deployment can still act on. We present Provenance-Aware Capability Enforcement (PACE), which mediates every tool call immediately before it executes. Path
case_studies.summary: Tool‑using LLM agents can be misdirected by poisoned tool data or memory, leading to unsafe actions. PACE intercepts every tool call, checks its provenance and context before execution, and blocks unsafe calls. This reduces the risk of unintended behaviour in automated systems using LLMs.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that runs LLM‑based automation, add a PACE‑style middleware to your tool‑execution pipeline: 1) Log the provenance of each tool (source, version, checksum). 2) Before calling the tool, verify the provenance against an approved catalogue. 3) Block or audit any call that fails the check.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a provenance-aware enforcement mechanism for tool‑using LLM agents, which is novel and directly addresses security and operational concerns when deploying LLMs that invoke external tools. IT engineers working with LLM APIs, agentic systems, and MLOps could integrate such a guard to mitigate malicious or unintended tool usage. The methodology is actionable within 90 days for those with existing LLM deployments, enabling them to build a middleware component to intercept tool calls and verify provenance before execution. Thus it scores moderately high on novelty and relevance, and offers practical value for near‑term implementation.
